Abstract.

Let KK be a rationally null-homologous knot in a three-manifold YY. We construct a version of knot Floer homology in this context, including a description of the Floer homology of a three-manifold obtained as Morse surgery on the knot KK. As an application, we express the Heegaard Floer homology of rational surgeries on YY along a null-homologous knot KK in terms of the filtered homotopy type of the knot invariant for KK. This has applications to Dehn surgery problems for knots in S3S^{3}. In a different direction, we use the techniques developed here to calculate the Heegaard Floer homology of an arbitrary Seifert fibered three-manifold.

1. Introduction

Heegaard Floer homology [24] is an invariant for closed, oriented three-manifolds YY, taking the form of a collection of homology groups which are functorial under cobordisms. In [22] and [27], this invariant is extended to an invariant for null-homologous knots KK. (Here, we say that a knot is null-homologous if its induced homology class in H1​(Y,ℤ)H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}) is trivial. If the induced homology class of a knot K⊂YK\subset Y in H1​(Y,ℚ)H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Q}) is trivial, we call the knot rationally null-homologous.) The knot invariant takes the form of a ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtration of the chain complex whose homology calculates the Heegaard Floer complex for YY. It is the filtered chain homotopy type of this filtered complex which depends on the particular knot KK.

The knot filtration gives rise to collection of chain complexes {As+​(K)}s∈ℤ\{{A}^{+}_{s}(K)\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}} and chain maps {vs+:As+​(K)⟶B+}s∈ℤ\{v^{+}_{s}\colon{A}^{+}_{s}(K)\longrightarrow{B}^{+}\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}} and {hs+:As+​(K)⟶B+}s∈ℤ\{h^{+}_{s}\colon{A}^{+}_{s}(K)\longrightarrow{B}^{+}\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}, where here B+=C​F+​(Y){B}^{+}=CF^{+}(Y) is a chain complex whose homology is the Heegaard Floer homology H​F+​(Y)HF^{+}(Y). Indeed, the homology groups of the chain complex As+​(K){A}^{+}_{s}(K) represents the homology H​F+HF^{+} of sufficiently large integer surgeries on YY along KK, in a sense which can be made precise (c.f. Theorem  of [22] and also [27]). (These complexes are defined in a more general setting in Section 3.)

Suppose that KK is a null-homologous knot in a three-manifold YY. Given a rational number rr, let Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) denote the three-manifold obtained by Dehn filling Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K) with a solid torus with slope rr (with respect to the canonical Seifert framing of KK). In the case where rr is an integer, the Heegaard Floer homology of Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) can described in terms of the above-mentioned data coming from the knot filtration, according to [25].

The primary aim of this article is to generalize this construction to the case of Morse surgery on a knot K⊂YK\subset Y which is only rationally null-homologous. (By Morse surgery, we mean here Dehn surgery on a knot which can be realized as the boundary of a single two-handle addition to [0,1]×Y[0,1]\times Y; in the case where KK is null-homologous, this corresponds to Dehn surgery with an integral slope). This construction has new consequences even in the case of null-homologous knots in a three-manifold: since the result of Dehn surgery on a null-homologous knot K⊂YK\subset Y can be viewed as Morse surgery on a knot in the connected sum of YY with a lens space, we obtain a description of the Heegaard Floer homology of Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) in terms of the original knot Floer homology of KK.

Rather than introducing the generalization of the knot package to knots which are only rationally null-homologous in this introduction, which will require some additional material in its statement (c.f. Sections 3, 5, and 6 below), we focus now in the description of the Floer homology of Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) when rr is a rational number, and K⊂YK\subset Y is null-homologous.

As a preliminary point, recall that the Heegaard Floer homology of YY admits a direct sum splitting indexed by the set of Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over YY, which in turn is an affine space for H2​(Y,ℤ)H^{2}(Y;\mathbb{Z}). In particular, if K⊂YK\subset Y is a knot in an integral homology sphere, then there is a splitting

H​F+​(Yp/q​(K))≅⨁i∈ℤ/p​ℤH​F+​(Yp/q​(K),i).HF^{+}(Y_{p/q}(K))\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb{Z}/{p}\mathbb{Z}}HF^{+}(Y_{p/q}(K),i).

Fix an integer ii, and consider the chain complexes

𝔸i+=⨁s∈ℤ(s,A⌊i+p​sq⌋+​(K))\displaystyle{\mathbb{A}}^{+}_{i}=\bigoplus_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}(s,{A}^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}(K)) and 𝔹i+=⨁s∈ℤ(s,B+),\displaystyle{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{i}=\bigoplus_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}(s,{B}^{+}),

where here ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor denotes the greatest integer smaller than or equal to xx, and all B⌊i+p​sq⌋+=C​F+​(Y){B}^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}=CF^{+}(Y) . We view the above chain homomorphisms v+v^{+} and h+h^{+} as maps

v+:(s,A⌊i+p​sq⌋+​(K))⟶(s,B+)\displaystyle v^{+}\colon(s,{A}^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}(K))\longrightarrow(s,{B}^{+}) and h+:(s,A⌊i+p​sq⌋+​(K))⟶(s−1,B+).\displaystyle h^{+}\colon(s,{A}^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}(K))\longrightarrow(s-1,{B}^{+}).

Adding these up, we obtain a chain map

Di,p/q+:𝔸i+⟶𝔹i+;D^{+}_{i,p/q}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{+}_{i}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{i};

i.e.

Di,p/q+​{(s,as)}s∈ℤ={(s,bs)}s∈ℤ,D^{+}_{i,p/q}\{(s,a_{s})\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}=\{(s,b_{s})\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}},

where here

bs=v⌊i+p​sq⌋+​(as)+h⌊i+p⁡(s−1)q⌋+​(as−1).b_{s}=v^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}(a_{s})+h^{+}_{\lfloor\frac{i+p(s-1)}{q}\rfloor}(a_{s-1}).

Let 𝕏i,p/q+{\mathbb{X}}^{+}_{i,p/q} denote the mapping cone of Di,p/q+D^{+}_{i,p/q}. Note that 𝕏i,p/q+{\mathbb{X}}^{+}_{i,p/q} depends on ii only through its congruence class modulo pp. Note also that As+{A}^{+}_{s} and Bs+{B}^{+}_{s} are relatively ℤ\mathbb{Z}-graded, and the homomorphisms vs+v^{+}_{s} and hs+h^{+}_{s} respect this relative grading. The mapping cone 𝕏i+{\mathbb{X}}^{+}_{i} can be endowed with a relative grading, with the convention that Di,p/q+D^{+}_{i,p/q} drops the grading by one.

This mapping cone, whose ingredients are extracted from the knot filtration, captures Heegaard Floer homology of p/qp/q surgeries on YY along KK, according to the following:

Theorem 1.1.

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a null-homologous knot, and let pp, qq be a pair of relatively prime integers. Then, for each i∈ℤ/p​ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}/{p}\mathbb{Z}, there is a relatively graded isomorphism of groups

H∗​(𝕏i,p/q+)≅H​F+​(Yp/q​(K),i).H_{*}({\mathbb{X}}^{+}_{i,p/q})\cong HF^{+}(Y_{p/q}(K),i).

The proof of Theorem 1.1 is based on generalization of the the knot filtration of [22] and [27] to the case of rationally null-homologous knots, together with a generalization of the integer surgeries description from [25] (where in fact Theorem 1.1 is proved in the case where q=1q=1). Note that in the more general case, the knot filtration is naturally a filtration by relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures on the knot complement (rather than integers). Rational surgeries on K⊂YK\subset Y can be realized as Morse surgeries on a knot in the connected sum of YY with a lens space. The resulting knot is gotten by forming the connected sum of KK with a model (homologically non-trivial) knot in the lens space. Theorem 1.1 is then realized as a combination of a straighforward calculation involving this model knot, combined with a Künneth principle for connected sums, followed by the general Morse surgeries description.

We turn now to various applications of Theorem 1.1.

1.1. Applications to knots with LL-space surgeries

In Section 8, we give applications of Theorem 1.1 to knots in S3S^{3} which admit LL-space surgeries.

Recall that an LL-space is a rational homology three-sphere YY whose Floer homology H​F+HF^{+} in each Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure is isomorphic (as a relatively-graded ℤ⁡[U]\mathbb{Z}[U]-module) to H​F+​(S3)HF^{+}(S^{3}). This is equivalent to the condition that H​F^​(Y,𝔰)≅ℤ\widehat{HF}(Y,\mathfrak{s})\cong\mathbb{Z} for each 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y). Recall also [14], [17] that if YY is a rational homology three-sphere, then H​F^​(Y,𝔰)\widehat{HF}(Y,\mathfrak{s}) is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-graded group. Thus, the Heegaard Floer homology of an LL-space is determined by the “correction term” function

d:Spinc​(Y)⟶ℚd\colon{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y)\longrightarrow\mathbb{Q}

which associates to each 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y) the degree in which H​F^​(Y,𝔰)\widehat{HF}(Y,\mathfrak{s}) is supported, compare also [6].

The set of LL-spaces includes all lens spaces and indeed all three-manifolds with elliptic geometry, c.f. [16]; for more examples, see also [12]. Another interesting family is given by the branched double-covers of alternating knots in S3S^{3}, c.f. [20].

Let K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} be a knot in the three-sphere. Write its symmetrized Alexander polynomial as

ΔK​(T)=a0+∑i>0ai​(Ti+T−i),\Delta_{K}(T)=a_{0}+\sum_{i>0}a_{i}(T^{i}+T^{-i}),

and let

(1) ti​(K)=∑j=1∞j​a|i|+j.t_{i}(K)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}ja_{|i|+j}.

Note that for any knot CC in S3S^{3}, there is a canonical affine map ℤ/p​ℤ≅Spinc​(Sp/q3​(C))\mathbb{Z}/{p}\mathbb{Z}\cong{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(S^{3}_{p/q}(C)).

Theorem 1.2.

Let K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} be a knot which admits an LL-space surgery, for some r=pq∈ℚr=\frac{p}{q}\in\mathbb{Q} with r≥0r\geq 0. Then, for all integers ii with |i|≤p2​q|i|\leq\frac{p}{2q} we have that

(2) d⁡(Sp/q3​(K),i)−d⁡(Sp/q3​(O),i)=−2​t⌊|i|q⌋​(K),d(S^{3}_{p/q}(K),i)-d(S^{3}_{p/q}(O),i)=-2t_{\lfloor\frac{|i|}{q}\rfloor}(K),

while for all |i|>p2​q|i|>\frac{p}{2q}, we have that ti​(K)=0t_{i}(K)=0.

In the case where q=1q=1, a version of the above theorem is established in [17] (c.f. Theorem  of [17]). Theorem 1.2 (in the case where q=2q=2) also gives the symmetry used in [15] to find an obstruction to a knot having unknotting number equal to one.

The following is a quick consequence of this result, together with the fact that knot Floer homology distinguishes the unknot (c.f. [21]) (though alternative proofs could be given which model the proof in [9] more closely):

Corollary 1.3.

If Sp/q3​(K)≅Sp/q3​(O)S^{3}_{p/q}(K)\cong S^{3}_{p/q}(O) as oriented three-manifolds, then K=OK=O.

The above result, which was conjectured by Gordon in [8], was first established using Seiberg-Witten monopoles in [9]. Thanks to a theorem of Eliashberg and Etnyre (c.f. [4] and [5]), it is now possible to prove results of this type purely in the context of Heegaard Floer homology, see also [21].

1.2. On cosmetic surgeries

Let YY be a closed, oriented three-manifold, and K⊂YK\subset Y be a framed knot. Given a rational number rr, let Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) denote the three-manifold obtained by Dehn surgery along KK with slope rr (with respect to the initial framing). If there are two distinct rational numbers rr and ss with the property that Yr​(K)Y_{r}(K) and Ys​(K)Y_{s}(K) are homeomorphic (but the homeomorphism is not required to preserve the orientation inherited from YY), then the surgeries are called cosmetic. A pair of surgeries on KK with r≠sr\neq s is called truly cosmetic if Yr​(K)≅Ys​(K)Y_{r}(K)\cong Y_{s}(K) as oriented manifolds.

Amphicheiral knots have cosmetic surgeries; specifically, if KK is an amphicheiral knot, then Sr3​(K)≅−S−r3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong-S^{3}_{-r}(K). The unknot OO admits infinitely many truly cosmetic surgeries: Sp/q3​(O)=Sp/p+q3​(O)S^{3}_{p/q}(O)=S^{3}_{p/{p+q}}(O). Lackenby [10] has shown that under general conditions on a knot K⊂YK\subset Y, there are at most finitely many cosmetic surgeries, see also [2]. It is conjectured [2] that if Yr​(K)≅Ys​(K)Y_{r}(K)\cong Y_{s}(K), then Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K) admits an automorphism which carries the slope rr to the slope ss.

The present state of Heegaard Floer homology – and specifically the surgery formulas given here – work best for excluding cosmetic surgeries on knots in S3S^{3}. For example, we have the following result:

Theorem 1.4.

If KK is a knot with Seifert genus equal to one, and Sr3​(K)≅Ss3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong S^{3}_{s}(K) with r≠sr\neq s, then Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) is an LL-space.

The conclusion of the above theorem places severe restrictions on KK. In particular, according to results of [16], it follows that KK must have the same knot Floer homology (and in particular the same Alexander poylnomial) as the trefoil knot TT, and thus according to Theorem 1.1, Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) and Sr3​(T)S^{3}_{r}(T) have the same (graded) Floer homology groups. For particular integers pp, the existence of a truly cosmetic surgery on such a knot KK with specified numerator pp can be ruled out by an explicit, finite search.

Theorem 1.5.

Let K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} and suppose that Sr3​(K)≅±Ss3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong\pm S^{3}_{s}(K), then either Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) is an LL-space or rr and ss have opposite signs.

For the above theorem, both possible conclusions can hold. The simplest example is the unknot which admits cosmetic surgeries with positive slopes. A more interesting example of cosmetic surgeries with positive slopes is provided by the trefoil knot KK, which has the property that S93​(K)≅−S9/23​(K)S^{3}_{9}(K)\cong-S^{3}_{9/2}(K), c.f. [11]. Examples where rr and ss have opposite signs are given by amphicheiral knots.

Our methods can be refined to exclude cosmetic surgeries for certain numerators pp. We study here the case where p=3p=3.

Theorem 1.6.

Suppose that K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a knot with the property that Sp/q3​(K)≅Sp/q′3​(K)S^{3}_{p/q}(K)\cong S^{3}_{p/q^{\prime}}(K) as oriented manifolds. In the case where p=3p=3, we can conclude that q=q′q=q^{\prime}.

1.3. Heegaard Floer homology of Seifert fibered spaces

We give some other applications of the general surgeries description along a rationally null-homologous knot. In Section 10, we use it to describe the Heegaard Floer homology of any Seifert fibered space whose first Betti number is even.

1.4. Organization

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review some of the topological preliminaries required by the knot filtrations, including the notion of relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures for three-manifolds with torus boundary. In Section 3, we give the construction of the knot filtration. In the next two sections, we turn to some properties of the knot Floer homology which are rather straightforward adaptations of the corresponding results for null-homologous knots ([22], [27]): the relationship between knot Floer homology and “large” surgeries on a rationally null-homologous knot (Section 4), and the Künneth principle for connected sums of knots (Section 5). The first result is an ingredient in the Morse surgery formula from Section 6. In Section 7, we show how the Künneth principle, together with the Morse surgery formula, give the rational surgery formula described in this introduction. In Section 8, we turn to knots which admit LL-space surgeries. In Section 9, we give the applications of the rational surgery formula to the problem of cosmetic surgeries on a knot in S3S^{3}. In Section 10, we turn to the Heegaard Floer homology groups of Seifert fibered spaces with even first Betti number.

1.5. Acknowledgements

The authors would like to thank Yi Ni, András Stipsicz, and Jacob Rasmussen for interesting conversations during the course of this work. We are also very grateful to Walter Neumann for sharing with us his expertise in hyperbolic geometry.

2. Preliminaries

We recall some of the background material and notation which will be required for the construction of the knot filtration. The bulk of this material is about the constructions relating (doubly-pointed) Heegaard diagrams for knots, and relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures for three-manifolds with boundary. We include also a few key properties of Heegaard Floer homology which will be used repeatedly throughout, see also [24].

2.1. Surgeries

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a knot. the boundary of a tubular neighborhood of the knot KK is a torus TT equipped with a canonical choice of (isotopy class of) embedded curve μ\mu, a meridian for KK. A longitude for KK is any embedded curve λ\lambda in TT which meets a meridian transversally in a single point.

Given a homologically non-trivial, embedded curve γ\gamma in TT, we can form the three-manifold Yγ​(K)Y_{\gamma}(K) which is gotten by attaching a solid torus to Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K) so that γ\gamma bounds a disk in the attached solid torus. We say that Yγ​(K)Y_{\gamma}(K) is obtained from YY by Dehn surgery along KK. In the special case where γ\gamma is a longitude for KK, there is a canonical two-handle cobordism from YY to Yγ​(K)Y_{\gamma}(K), and we say that Yγ​(K)Y_{\gamma}(K) is obtained from YY by Morse surgery on KK. A choice of longitude for KK is also called a framing of KK.

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a rationally null-homologous knot in a closed, oriented three-manifold, equipped with a framing λ\lambda. Since K∈YK\in Y has finite order, there is a pair of integers nn and dd with minimal absolute value which satisfy the property that

(3) d⋅λ=n⋅μ∈H1​(Y−K,ℤ),d\cdot\lambda=n\cdot\mu\in H_{1}(Y-K;\mathbb{Z}),

In particular, it follows that the induced homology class [Kλ]∈H1​(Y,ℤ)[K_{\lambda}]\in H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z}) has order |d||d|. Here, and in the future, KλK_{\lambda} denotes a copy of KK displaced into Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K) using the framing λ\lambda.

2.2. Relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures for three-manifolds with boundary

Following Turaev [30], we say that two vector fields v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} on a closed, oriented three-manifold are homologous if they are homotopic in the complement of a ball in YY. The set of homology classes of vector fields can be given the structure of an affine space for H2​(Y,ℤ)H^{2}(Y;\mathbb{Z}), and indeed, it can be identified with the space of Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over YY, Spinc​(Y){\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y).

This construction can be readily generalized to the case of a three-manifold with torus boundary, c.f. Chapter I.4 of [30]. Specifically, on an oriented three-manifold MM with torus boundary, two vector fields v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} on MM which vanish nowhere and point outwards at ∂M\partial M are said to be homologous if they are homotopic in the complement of a ball in the interior of MM. The set of homology classes of nowhere vanishing vector fields can be naturally given the structure of an affine space for the relative cohomology H2​(M,∂M,ℤ)H^{2}(M,\partial M;\mathbb{Z}). The homology classes of nowhere vanishing vector fields are called relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures on MM, and are denoted Spinc¯​(M,∂M)\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(M,\partial M).

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a knot in a closed, oriented three-manifold, we can construct the three-manifold with torus boundary M=Y−nd⁡(K)M=Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K). In this case, we denote the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over MM by Spinc¯​(Y,K)\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K).

Orienting the core of the solid torus, we obtain a canonical isotopy class of nowhere vanishing vector field which points inward at the boundary, and which has a closed orbit which is the core of the solid torus (with its given orientation). More explicitly, the isotopy class of this vector field on D2×S1D^{2}\times S^{1} is characterized by the property that in the interior of the solid torus, ww is everywhere transverse to the tangent planes to D2D^{2}.

Giving KK an orientation (and denoting this oriented knot by K¯\overline{K}), we glue in this vector field ww to obtain a natural map

GY,K¯:Spinc¯​(Y,K)⟶Spinc​(Y)G_{Y,\overline{K}}\colon\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K)\longrightarrow{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y)

which is equivariant with respect to the action by H2​(Y,K,ℤ)H^{2}(Y,K;\mathbb{Z}); i.e. letting

ι:H2​(Y,K,ℤ)⟶H2​(Y,ℤ)\iota\colon H^{2}(Y,K;\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow H^{2}(Y;\mathbb{Z})

be the natural map, we have for each k∈H2​(Y,K,ℤ)k\in H^{2}(Y,K;\mathbb{Z}),

GY,K¯​(ξ+k)=GY,K¯​(ξ)+ι⁡(k).G_{Y,\overline{K}}(\xi+k)=G_{Y,\overline{K}}(\xi)+\iota(k).

As the notation suggests, GY,K¯G_{Y,\overline{K}} depends on the orientation for KK; indeed, for any ξ∈Spinc​(Y,K)\xi\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y,K),

(4) GY,K¯​(ξ)−GY,−K¯​(ξ)=PD⁡[K¯].G_{Y,\overline{K}}(\xi)-G_{Y,-\overline{K}}(\xi)=\mathrm{PD}[\overline{K}].

Note that if YY is a three-manifold, and K⊂YK\subset Y is a knot with meridian μ\mu, then the fibers of the map GY,K¯G_{Y,\overline{K}} are the orbits of Spinc¯​(Y,K)\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K) under the action by ℤ⋅PD⁡[μ]\mathbb{Z}\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu], where we think of PD⁡[μ]∈H2​(Y,K,ℤ)\mathrm{PD}[\mu]\in H^{2}(Y,K;\mathbb{Z}); i.e. GY,K¯G_{Y,\overline{K}} realizes an identification

Spinc​(Y)≅Spinc¯​(Y,K)ℤ⋅PD⁡[μ].{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y)\cong\frac{\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K)}{\mathbb{Z}\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu]}.

2.3. Doubly-pointed Heegaard diagrams

A doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram is a collection of data (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z) where Σ\Sigma is an oriented surface of genus gg, 𝜶={α1,…,αg}\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}=\{\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{g}\} is a gg-tuple of homologically linearly independent, pairwise disjoint, embedded curves in Σ\Sigma (a gg-tuple of attaching circles), and 𝜷={β1,…,βg}\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}=\{\beta_{1},...,\beta_{g}\} is another gg-tuple of attaching circles, and ww and zz are two distinct pair of points in Σ−α1−…−αg−β1−…−βg\Sigma-\alpha_{1}-...-\alpha_{g}-\beta_{1}-...-\beta_{g}.

A doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram gives rise to an oriented three-manifold YY together with an oriented knot K¯⊂Y\overline{K}\subset Y. The orientation on Σ\Sigma induces an orientation on UαU_{\alpha} (so that ∂Uα=Σ\partial U_{\alpha}=\Sigma), which can then be uniquely extended to an orientation over YY. The knot KK is obtained as a union of two arcs, ηα\eta_{\alpha} and ηβ\eta_{\beta}. The arc ηα\eta_{\alpha} is gotten by connecting ww and zz in Σ−α1−…−αg\Sigma-\alpha_{1}-...-\alpha_{g}, and orienting it as a path from ww to zz. This arc is then pushed into UαU_{\alpha} so that only its boundary meets Σ\Sigma (at ww and zz). The arc ηβ\eta_{\beta} is obtained in an analogous manner, only reversing the roles of the circles in 𝜶\alpha and 𝜷\beta. The oriented knot K¯\overline{K} is gotten by the difference ηα−ηβ\eta_{\alpha}-\eta_{\beta}.

2.4. Relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures associated to intersection points

Let (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z) be a doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram. Fix 𝐱,𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}. There are paths

a:[0,1]⟶𝕋α,b:[0,1]⟶𝕋βa\colon[0,1]\longrightarrow{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha},b\colon[0,1]\longrightarrow{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}

with ∂a=∂b=𝐱−𝐲\partial a=\partial b=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}. These paths can be viewed as arcs in Σ\Sigma (supported inside the 𝜶∪𝜷\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}\cup\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}). The difference a−ba-b is a closed one-cycle in Σ\Sigma which is disjoint from ww and zz. Indeed, since Σ−w−z\Sigma-w-z is a subset of Y−KY-K, this one-cycle can be viewed as an element ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐲)∈H1​(Y−K,ℤ){\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\in H_{1}(Y-K;\mathbb{Z}).

We construct a map

𝔰¯w,z:𝕋α∩𝕋β⟶Spinc¯​(Y,K),\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}\colon{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}\longrightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K),

as follows (compare the analogous construction from [24]). A Heegaard diagram (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z) can be realized by a self-indexing Morse function f:Y⟶[0,3]f\colon Y\longrightarrow[0,3], with a single index zero and three critical point (and gg index one and two critical points), together with a Riemannian metric gg, for which Σ\Sigma is the mid-level f−1​(3/2)f^{-1}(3/2), αi\alpha_{i} is the locus of points flowing out of the it​hi^{th} index one critical point (via gradient flow), and βj\beta_{j} is the locus of points flowing into the jt​hj^{th} index two critical point. Thus, 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta} can be thought of as a gg-tuple of gradient flow-lines γ𝐱\gamma_{\mathbf{x}} containing all the index one and two critical points.

Now, the knot KK is realized as a union of two flow-lines γw\gamma_{w} and γz\gamma_{z} which connect the index zero and index three critical points, meeting Σ\Sigma in the points ww and zz respectively. The oriented knot K¯\overline{K} is gotten by γz−γw\gamma_{z}-\gamma_{w}.

We construct a vector field representing the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure 𝔰¯w,z​(ξ)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\xi) as follows. Modify the gradient vector field ∇→​f\vec{\nabla}f in a neighborhood of the flows γ𝐱\gamma_{\mathbf{x}} so that it has no zeros at any of the index one or two critical points. This modification involves a choice of nowhere vanishing vector field in a regular neighborhood of γ𝐱\gamma_{\mathbf{x}}, but it will follow easily from the construction that this choice will not affect the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure of the induced vector field. Next, we modify the vector field in a neighborhood of γw\gamma_{w} to obtain a new vector field vv which has no zeros at either the index zero or three-critical points. In fact, this can be achieved so that the knot KK is a closed orbit of the resulting vector field, whose orientation as a flow-line agrees with the orientation induced from K¯\overline{K}. This vv modification involves a choice XX of nowhere vanishing vector field on the neighborhood of γw\gamma_{w}, with fixed behaviour on KK. When calling attention to this choice, we write v=v⁡(X)v=v(X). The resulting vector field vv over YY is the vector field representing the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure 𝔰w​(𝐱)∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\mathbf{x})\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y) associated to the intersection point 𝐱\mathbf{x} and reference point ww, as described in [24] (and this fact is independent of the choice of XX).

Our representative vv has been constructed so that there is a neighborhood D2×S1D_{2}\times S^{1} of the closed flow-line {0}×S1≅K¯\{0\}\times S^{1}\cong\overline{K} (where here D2D_{2} is a disk of radius two centered at the origin) with the property that the disks D2×θD_{2}\times\theta for any θ∈S1\theta\in S^{1} are transverse to the vector field vv. Consider a concentric disk D1⊂D2D_{1}\subset D_{2}. We can continuously extend v2=v|Y−D2×S1v_{2}=v|_{Y-D_{2}\times S^{1}} to a new vector field v1=v1​(𝐱,X)v_{1}=v_{1}(\mathbf{x},X) over Y−D1×S1Y-D_{1}\times S^{1}, by using a vector field over (D2−D1)×S1(D_{2}-D_{1})\times S^{1} which is everywhere transverse to the annuli (D2−D1)×θ(D_{2}-D_{1})\times\theta, and which point towards the origin at ∂D1×S1\partial D_{1}\times S^{1}. Thus, the vector field v1v_{1} over Y−(D1×S1)Y-(D_{1}\times S^{1}) inherits the vector field v′v^{\prime} which points outwards at the boundary. It is easy to see that the isotopy class of v1v_{1} is uniquely determined by the isotopy class of our initial vector field vv.

The induced relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure v1v_{1} over Y−nd⁡(()​K)=Y−(D1×S1)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(()K)=Y-(D_{1}\times S^{1}) depends, of course, on ww, zz, 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and our choice XX, and we write it correspondingly as v1​(w,z,𝐱,X)v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X). It is easy to see that

GY,K¯​(v1​(w,z,𝐱,X))=𝔰w​(𝐱).G_{Y,\overline{K}}(v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X))=\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\mathbf{x}).

It is easy to see that the induced relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K) depends on the choice of XX by

v1​(w,z,𝐱,X)−v1​(w,z,𝐱,X′)=a⋅PD⁡[μ],v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X)-v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X^{\prime})=a\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu],

where here a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} is a universal constant (depending on only XX and X′X^{\prime}; in fact, it is even independent of the ambient three-manifold YY). We choose XX now to satisfy a normalization condition as follows.

Consider the unknot K⊂S3K\subset S^{3}. An orientation K¯\overline{K} specifies a canonical relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure 𝔰¯0∈Spinc¯​(S3,K¯)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{0}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(S^{3},\overline{K}). This is the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure represented by a vector field vv over S3−nd⁡(K¯)≅D2×S1S^{3}-{\mathrm{nd}}(\overline{K})\cong D^{2}\times S^{1} which is everywhere transverse to the disks D2D^{2}. The direction is specified by the condition that vv can be represented by a vector field with closed orbits which have linking number one with our original knot K¯\overline{K}. Our condition on XX now is that for the standard genus one doubly-pointed diagram for the oriented unknot with a single intersection point 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure induced by v1​(w,z,𝐱,X)v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X) is the canonical Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure for the oriented unknot.

With this choice for XX, it is easy now to see that the relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure underlying v1​(w,z,𝐱,X)v_{1}(w,z,\mathbf{x},X) depends only on ww, zz, and 𝐱\mathbf{x}, inducing the required map 𝔰¯w,z:𝕋α∩𝕋β⟶Spinc¯​(Y,K)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}\colon{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}\longrightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K).

We investigate its dependence on ww, zz, and 𝐱\mathbf{x} in the following lemma. Continuing notation from [24], letting 𝐱,𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}, let π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) denote the space of homotopy classes of Whitney disks connecting 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐲\mathbf{y}, and for fixed

p∈Σ−α1−…−αg−β1−…−βgp\in\Sigma-\alpha_{1}-...-\alpha_{g}-\beta_{1}-...-\beta_{g}

and ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}), let np​(ϕ)n_{p}(\phi) denote the intersection number of ϕ\phi with the submanifold {p}×Symg−1​(Σ)⊂Symg​(Σ)\{p\}\times\mathrm{Sym}^{g-1}(\Sigma)\subset\mathrm{Sym}^{g}(\Sigma).

Lemma 2.1.

Given 𝐱,𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}, we have that

(5) 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐲)−𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)=PD⁡[ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐲)].\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{y})-\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{PD}[{\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})].

In particular, if there is some ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}), then

(6) 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)−𝔰¯w,z​(𝐲)=(nz​(ϕ)−nw​(ϕ))⋅PD⁡[μ].\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})-\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{y})=(n_{z}(\phi)-n_{w}(\phi))\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu].

Proof. We begin by establishing Equation (5). Vector fields representing 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}) and 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐲)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{y}) can be chosen so that they agree everywhere except in a regular neighborhood of ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐲){\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}). It follows that 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}) and 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐲)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{y}) differ by some multiple of the Poincaré dual of this curve (in the case where the curve is one). The fact that this multiple is one follows from the analgous property of 𝔰w​(𝐱)\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\mathbf{x}) established in Lemma  of [24].

We turn to Equation (6). The homotopy class ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) gives rise to a null-homotopy of ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐲){\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) inside YY. This null-homology meets the knot KK with intersection number nz​(ϕ)−nw​(ϕ)n_{z}(\phi)-n_{w}(\phi). Thus, it can be modified to give a homology of ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐲){\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) with (nz​(ψ)−nw​(ψ))⋅PD⁡[μ](n_{z}(\psi)-n_{w}(\psi))\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu] in Y−KY-K. Equation (6) now follows from Equation (5).           

2.5. Heegaard triples and relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures

A Heegaard triple is a closed, oriented two-manifold Σ\Sigma, equipped with three gg-tuples of attaching circles, (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,𝜸)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$}), c.f. [24]. This gives rise to a four-manifold Xα​β​γX_{\alpha\beta\gamma} which has three boundary components −Yα​β-Y_{\alpha\beta}, Yβ​γY_{\beta\gamma}, and Yα​γY_{\alpha\gamma}. (Of course, Yα​βY_{\alpha\beta} here denotes the three-manifold described by the Heegaard diagram (Σ,𝜶,𝜷)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}); Yα​γY_{\alpha\gamma} and Yβ​γY_{\beta\gamma} are defined analogously.)

Suppose K⊂YK\subset Y is a framed knot. We can construct a Heegaard triple (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,𝜸)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$}), where Yα​βY_{\alpha\beta} represents YY, Yα​γY_{\alpha\gamma} represents framed surgery along KK, and Yβ​γY_{\beta\gamma} is a connected sum of g−1g-1 copies of S2×S1S^{2}\times S^{1}, and filling in Yβ​γY_{\beta\gamma} by a boundary connected sum of g−1g-1 copies of B3×S1B^{3}\times S^{1}, we obtain a four-manifold which is diffeomorphic to Wλ​(K)W_{\lambda}(K). This is obtained by first writing down a Heegaard triple with the property that KK is supported entirely inside UβU_{\beta}, as the core of one of the handles in the handlebody, and βg\beta_{g} represents its meridian, and realizing the framing λ\lambda as a curve γg\gamma_{g} which is disjoint from the βi\beta_{i} for i=1,…,g−1i=1,...,g-1. We then let γi\gamma_{i} for i=1,…,g−1i=1,...,g-1 be small, isotopic translates of the corresponding βi\beta_{i}. We would like to choose convenient reference points. These are points ww and zz are chosen so that there is an arc from zz to ww which crosses none of the αi\alpha_{i} or γi\gamma_{i} for i=1,…,gi=1,...,g, or βj\beta_{j} for j=1,…,g−1j=1,...,g-1, so that an arc from zz to ww crosses βg\beta_{g} transverally once. An ordering on ww and zz is specified by an orientation on KK We call such a doubly-pointed Heegaard triple (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,𝜸,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$},w,z) to be a doubly-pointed Heegaard triple subordinate to the framed, oriented knot K¯⊂Y\overline{K}\subset Y with framing λ\lambda.

By constructing the diagram carefully, we can arrange for there to be a unique intersection point Θ∈𝕋β∩𝕋γ\Theta\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma} representing the generator Θ\Theta of the top-most non-trivial Floer homology group of H​F^​(#g−1​(S2×S1))\widehat{HF}(\#^{g-1}(S^{2}\times S^{1})). We denote this intersection point, and its corresponding homology class, by Θ\Theta.

As in [24], we let π2​(𝐱,Θ,𝐲)\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\Theta,\mathbf{y}) denote the space of homotopy classes of Whitney triangles, i.e. continuous maps of the triangle into Symg​(Σ)\mathrm{Sym}^{g}(\Sigma) which map the three edges to 𝕋α{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}, 𝕋β{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}, and 𝕋γ{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma}, and the vertices to the given points. In Section  of [24], it is shown that homotopy classes of triangles give rise to Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over Xα,β,γX_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}.

Proposition 2.2.

Let (Σ,𝛂,𝛃,𝛄,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$},w,z) be a doubly-pointed Heegaard triple subordinate to an oriented knot K¯⊂Y\overline{K}\subset Y, equipped with framing λ\lambda. The map

ψ∈π2​(𝐱,Θ,𝐲)↦𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)+(nw​(ψ)−nz​(ψ))​μ\psi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\Theta,\mathbf{y})\mapsto\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})+(n_{w}(\psi)-n_{z}(\psi))\mu

descends to give a well-defined map

EY,λ,K¯:Spinc​(Wλ​(K))⟶Spinc¯​(Y,K¯)E_{Y,\lambda,\overline{K}}\colon{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(W_{\lambda}(K))\longrightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,\overline{K})

(i.e. which is independent of the choice of Heegaard triple). Moreover, letting F^∈H2​(Wλ​(K),Y)≅ℤ\widehat{F}\in H_{2}(W_{\lambda}(K),Y)\cong\mathbb{Z} denote a generator, we have that

(7) EY,λ,K¯​(𝔰+PD⁡[Fλ])=EY,λ,K¯​(𝔰)+PD⁡[Kλ].E_{Y,\lambda,\overline{K}}(\mathfrak{s}+\mathrm{PD}[F_{\lambda}])=E_{Y,\lambda,\overline{K}}(\mathfrak{s})+\mathrm{PD}[K_{\lambda}].

Proof. Recall [24] that two triangles ψ∈π2​(𝐱,Θ,𝐲)\psi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\Theta,\mathbf{y}) and ψ′∈π2​(𝐱′,Θ,𝐲′)\psi^{\prime}\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\Theta,\mathbf{y}^{\prime}) induce the same Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure on Wλ​(K)W_{\lambda}(K) is and only if there are ϕ1∈π2​(𝐱,𝐱′)\phi_{1}\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) (relative to the subspaces 𝕋α{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha} and 𝕋β{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}) and ϕ2∈π2​(𝐲′,𝐲)\phi_{2}\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime},\mathbf{y}) (relative to the subspaces 𝕋α{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha} and 𝕋γ{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma}) with the property that

𝒟⁡(ψ)−𝒟⁡(ψ′)−𝒟⁡(ϕ1)−𝒟⁡(ϕ2)=n⋅[Σ]{\mathcal{D}}(\psi)-{\mathcal{D}}(\psi^{\prime})-{\mathcal{D}}(\phi_{1})-{\mathcal{D}}(\phi_{2})=n\cdot[\Sigma]

for some integer nn. (Here, as in [24], 𝒟⁡(ψ){\mathcal{D}}(\psi) denotes the two-chain in Σ\Sigma induced by the homotopy class ψ\psi, whose multiplicity at some point pp is the intersection number of ψ\psi with p×Symg−1​(Σ)p\times\mathrm{Sym}^{g-1}(\Sigma).) But now nw​(ϕ2)=nz​(ϕ2)n_{w}(\phi_{2})=n_{z}(\phi_{2}) (since ww and zz lie in the same component of Σ−α1−…−αg−γ1−…−γg\Sigma-\alpha_{1}-...-\alpha_{g}-\gamma_{1}-...-\gamma_{g}); combining this with the fact that

𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱′)=𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)+(nw​(ϕ1)−nz​(ϕ1))⋅μ\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})+(n_{w}(\phi_{1})-n_{z}(\phi_{1}))\cdot\mu

(Lemma 2.1), it follows that in this case

𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)+(nw​(ψ)−nz​(ψ))​μ=𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱′)+(nw​(ψ′)−nz​(ψ′))​μ.\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})+(n_{w}(\psi)-n_{z}(\psi))\mu=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})+(n_{w}(\psi^{\prime})-n_{z}(\psi^{\prime}))\mu.

Independence of the Heegaard triple is a routine consequence that any two Heegaard triples can be connected by a sequence of stabilizations and handleslides among the αi\alpha_{i}, βj\beta_{j} for j=1,…,g−1j=1,...,g-1, and the distinguished meridian βg\beta_{g} handlesliding over the other βj\beta_{j}.

We now verify Equation (7). Suppose that we have ψ∈π2​(𝐱,Θ,𝐲)\psi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\Theta,\mathbf{y}) and ψ′∈π2​(𝐱′,Θ,𝐲)\psi^{\prime}\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\Theta,\mathbf{y}). The difference 𝒟⁡(ψ)−𝒟⁡(ψ′){\mathcal{D}}(\psi)-{\mathcal{D}}(\psi^{\prime}) gives a two-chain CC in Σ\Sigma, which has no corners on γi\gamma_{i} for i=1,…,gi=1,...,g. The corners of CC occur at xi′∈𝐱′x_{i}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{x}^{\prime} and xi∈𝐱x_{i}\in\mathbf{x}. Indeed, the boundary of the two-chain consists of ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐱′){\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) and some number of copies of the γi\gamma_{i}. As such, it can be thought of as furnishing a homology

ϵ¯​(𝐱,𝐱′)=ℓ⋅γg+(nw​(ψ−ψ′)−nz​(ψ−ψ′))​μ{\underline{\epsilon}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\ell\cdot\gamma_{g}+(n_{w}(\psi-\psi^{\prime})-n_{z}(\psi-\psi^{\prime}))\mu

in the knot complement (we are thinking of λ\lambda as a curve in the Heegaard surface; of course, it is identified with KλK_{\lambda} thought of as a curve in the knot complement). Indeed, ψ−ψ′\psi-\psi^{\prime} corresponds to a surface-with-boundary ZZ in the four-manifold underlying the Heegaard triple, whose boundary is supported entirely YY. The integer ℓ\ell corresponds to the multiplicity with which ZZ meets the cocore of the attaching two-handle. Thus, 𝔰w​(ψ)−𝔰w​(ψ′)=ℓ⋅F^\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\psi)-\mathfrak{s}_{w}(\psi^{\prime})=\ell\cdot\widehat{F}, and the equation follows.           

For a pointed Heegaard triple (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,𝜸,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$},z), the group of two-dimensional homology classes is identified with the group of relations a+b+c=0a+b+c=0 in H1​(Σ,ℤ)H_{1}(\Sigma;\mathbb{Z}) where where aa resp. bb resp. cc lies in the span of {[αi]}i=1g\{[\alpha_{i}]\}_{i=1}^{g} resp. {[βi]}i=1g\{[\beta_{i}]\}_{i=1}^{g} resp. {[γi]}i=1g\{[\gamma_{i}]\}_{i=1}^{g}. These relations correspond to two-chains PP in Σ\Sigma with boundary a formal linear combination of the attaching circles, and with nz​(P)=0n_{z}(P)=0. Given a Whitney triangle ψ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲,𝐰)\psi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{w}), there is a formula for the evaluation ⟨c1​(𝔰z​(ψ)),[P]⟩\langle c_{1}(\mathfrak{s}_{z}(\psi)),[P]\rangle, where [P][P] denotes the second homology class corresponding to PP, in terms of the Heegaard triple, c.f. Proposition  of [14]. To describe this, we need two notions, the Euler measure of the periodic domain and the dual spider number of the triangle with respect to the triply-periodic domain.

Let Φ:F⟶Σ\Phi\colon F\longrightarrow\Sigma be a representative for PP, where here Φ\Phi is an immersion in a neighborhood of ∂F\partial F. The line bundle Φ∗​(T​Σ)\Phi^{*}(T\Sigma) has a canonical trivialization over ∂F\partial F, since Φ\Phi induces an isomorphism

T​F≅Φ∗​(T​Σ),TF\cong\Phi^{*}(T\Sigma),

and T​FTF is canonically trivialized near ∂F\partial F (using the outward normal orientation on FF). We define χ^​(𝒫)\widehat{\chi}({\mathcal{P}}) to be the Euler number of Φ∗​(T​Σ)\Phi^{*}(T\Sigma), relative to this trivialization at ∂F\partial F,

χ^​(𝒫)=⟨c1​(Φ∗​(T​Σ),∂F),F⟩.\widehat{\chi}({\mathcal{P}})=\langle c_{1}(\Phi^{*}(T\Sigma),\partial F),F\rangle.

Note first that the orientation of Σ\Sigma, and the orientations on all the attaching circles 𝜶\alpha, 𝜷\beta, and 𝜸\gamma naturally induce “inward” normal vector fields to the attaching circles (i.e. if γ:S1⟶Σ\gamma\colon S^{1}\longrightarrow\Sigma is a unit speed immersed curve, this inward normal vector is given by J​d​γd​tJ\frac{d\gamma}{dt}). Let αi′\alpha_{i}^{\prime}, βi′\beta_{i}^{\prime}, and γi′\gamma_{i}^{\prime} denote copies of the corresponding attaching circles αi′\alpha_{i}^{\prime}, βi′\beta_{i}^{\prime}, and γi′\gamma_{i}^{\prime}, translated slightly in these normal directions. Let 𝜶′\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}^{\prime}, 𝜷′\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}^{\prime}, and 𝜸′\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$}^{\prime} denote the corresponding gg-tuples, and 𝕋α′{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}, 𝕋β′{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}^{\prime}, and 𝕋γ′{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma}^{\prime} be the corresponding tori in Symg​(Σ)\mathrm{Sym}^{g}(\Sigma). By construction, then, u⁡(eα)u(e_{\alpha}) misses 𝕋α′{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}^{\prime}, u⁡(eβ)u(e_{\beta}) misses 𝕋β′{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}^{\prime}, and u⁡(eγ)u(e_{\gamma}) misses 𝕋γ′{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma}^{\prime}.

Let x∈Δx\in\Delta be a point in the interior, chosen in general position, so that the gg-tuple u⁡(x)u(x) misses all of 𝜶′\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}^{\prime}, 𝜷′\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}^{\prime}, and 𝜸′\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$}^{\prime}. Choose three paths aa, bb, and cc from xx to e0e_{0}, e1e_{1}, and e2e_{2} respectively. The central point xx and the three paths aa, bb, and cc is called a dual spider. We can think of the paths aa, bb, and cc as one-chains in Σ\Sigma. Recall that ∂𝒫\partial\mathcal{P} has three types of boundaries: the α\alpha, β\beta, and γ\gamma boundaries, which we denote ∂α𝒫\partial_{\alpha}\mathcal{P}, ∂β𝒫\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{P}, and ∂γ𝒫\partial_{\gamma}\mathcal{P}. Let ∂α′𝒫\partial^{\prime}_{\alpha}\mathcal{P}, ∂β′𝒫\partial^{\prime}_{\beta}\mathcal{P}, and ∂γ′𝒫\partial^{\prime}_{\gamma}\mathcal{P} respectively denote the one-chains obtained by translating the corresponding boundary components using the induced normal vector fields. The dual spider number of uu and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined by

σ⁡(u,𝒫)=nu⁡(x)​(𝒫)+#⁡(a∩∂α′𝒫)+#⁡(b∩∂β′𝒫)+#⁡(c∩∂γ′𝒫).\sigma(u,\mathcal{P})=n_{u(x)}(\mathcal{P})+\#(a\cap\partial^{\prime}_{\alpha}\mathcal{P})+\#(b\cap\partial^{\prime}_{\beta}\mathcal{P})+\#(c\cap\partial^{\prime}_{\gamma}\mathcal{P}).

According to Proposition  of [14],

(8) ⟨c1​(𝔰z​(u)),H⁡(𝒫)⟩=χ^​(𝒫)+#⁡(∂𝒫)−2​nz​(𝒫)+2​σ​(u,𝒫),\langle c_{1}(\mathfrak{s}_{z}(u)),H(\mathcal{P})\rangle=\widehat{\chi}(\mathcal{P})+\#(\partial\mathcal{P})-2n_{z}(\mathcal{P})+2\sigma(u,\mathcal{P}),

where here #⁡(∂𝒫)\#(\partial\mathcal{P}) represents the number of boundary components of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, with multiplicity.

2.6. Filtered complexes

A ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered complex is a chain complex CC whose underlying Abelian group decomposes as

C=⨁(i,j)∈ℤ⊕ℤC⁡{i,j},C=\bigoplus_{(i,j)\in\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}}C\{i,j\},

and whose boundary operator ∂\partial carries C​{i0,j0}C\{i_{0},j_{0}\} into the subset

C{i≤i0andj≤j0}=⨁{i′,j′|i′≤iandj′≤j}C{i′,j′}⊂C.C\{i\leq i_{0}~\text{and}~j\leq j_{0}\}=\bigoplus_{\{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\big|i^{\prime}\leq i~\text{and}~j^{\prime}\leq j\}}C\{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\}\subset C.

A map f:C⟶C′f\colon C\longrightarrow C^{\prime} between filtered complexes is called a filtered map if it carries C​{i0,j0}C\{i_{0},j_{0}\} into C′{i≤i0andj≤j0}C^{\prime}\{i\leq i_{0}~\text{and}~j\leq j_{0}\}. Two filtered chain maps

f0,f1:C⟶C′f_{0},f_{1}\colon C\longrightarrow C^{\prime}

are called filtered homotopic if there is a filtered map H:C⟶C′H\colon C\longrightarrow C^{\prime} with

f0−f1=∂′∘H+H∘∂.f_{0}-f_{1}=\partial^{\prime}\circ H+H\circ\partial.

Two filtered chain maps CC and C′C^{\prime} are called filtered chain homotopy equivalent if there are filtered chain maps f:C⟶C′f\colon C\longrightarrow C^{\prime} and g:C′⟶Cg\colon C^{\prime}\longrightarrow C with the property that f∘gf\circ g and g∘fg\circ f are filtered homotopic to the corresponding identity maps.

A ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered ℤ⁡[U]\mathbb{Z}[U]-complex CC is a filtered chain complex equipped with an endomorphism U:C⟶CU\colon C\longrightarrow C whose restriction to C​{i,j}C\{i,j\} maps to C​{i−1,j−1}C\{i-1,j-1\}.

If C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered ℤ⁡[U]\mathbb{Z}[U]-chain complexes, then we can form their tensor product C1⊗ℤ⁡[U]C2C_{1}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[U]}C_{2}. This can be given a ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtration by

(C⊗C′)​{i,j}=⨁{(i1,j1),(i2,j2)|(i1,j1)+(i2,j2)=(i,j)}C{i1,j1}⊗C{i2,j2}U1⋅ξ1⊗ξ2∼ξ1⊗U2⋅ξ2.(C\otimes C^{\prime})\{i,j\}=\frac{\bigoplus_{\{(i_{1},j_{1}),(i_{2},j_{2})\big|(i_{1},j_{1})+(i_{2},j_{2})=(i,j)\}}C\{i_{1},j_{1}\}\otimes C\{i_{2},j_{2}\}}{U_{1}\cdot\xi_{1}\otimes\xi_{2}\sim\xi_{1}\otimes U_{2}\cdot\xi_{2}}.

If CC is a filtered complex, and (a,b)∈ℤ⊕ℤ(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}, let C⁡[(a,b)]C[(a,b)] denote the filtered complex whose underlying chain complex is isomorphic, but whose filtration is shifted by (a,b)(a,b); i.e.

C⁡[(a,b)]​{i,j}=C⁡{a+i,b+j}.C[(a,b)]\{i,j\}=C\{a+i,b+j\}.

A relatively filtered map f:C⟶C′f\colon C\longrightarrow C^{\prime} is a chain map which respects the filtration on CC and the filtration C′​[(a,b)]C^{\prime}[(a,b)] for some (a,b)∈ℤ⊕ℤ(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}.

2.7. Absolute gradings

Heegaard Floer homology is natural under cobordisms. Indeed, if WW is a smooth, connected, oriented cobordism with ∂W=−Y1∪Y2\partial W=-Y_{1}\cup Y_{2} which is equipped with a Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure 𝔰\mathfrak{s} whose restriction 𝔱i=𝔰|Yi\mathfrak{t}_{i}=\mathfrak{s}|_{Y_{i}} for i=1,2i=1,2 has torsion first Chern class, then there is an induced chain map

fW,𝔰+:C​F+​(Y1,𝔱1)⟶C​F+​(Y2,𝔱2)f^{+}_{W,\mathfrak{s}}\colon CF^{+}(Y_{1},\mathfrak{t}_{1})\longrightarrow CF^{+}(Y_{2},\mathfrak{t}_{2})

which is homogeneous of degree

(9) c1​(𝔰)2−2​χ​(W)−3​σ​(W)4\frac{c_{1}(\mathfrak{s})^{2}-2\chi(W)-3\sigma(W)}{4}

(c.f. Theorem  of [14]).

Let 𝒯+{\mathcal{T}}^{+} denote the module ℤ⁡[U,U−1]/U⋅ℤ⁡[U]\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}]/U\cdot\mathbb{Z}[U]. Recall [24] that H​F+​(S3)≅𝒯+HF^{+}(S^{3})\cong{\mathcal{T}}^{+}. The ℚ\mathbb{Q}-grading on Floer homology is characterized by Equation (9), together with the normalization that H​Fd+​(S3)HF^{+}_{d}(S^{3}) is trivial for all d<0d<0, non-trivial in degree d=0d=0.

Following our usual notational conventions, we write 𝒯(d)+{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{(d)} for the module 𝒯+{\mathcal{T}}^{+}, thought of as a graded ℤ⁡[U]\mathbb{Z}[U]-module, where multiplication by UU lowers absolute degree by 22, and the non-zero homogeneous elements of lowest degree have degree dd. In this notation, then, H​F+​(S3)≅𝒯(0)+HF^{+}(S^{3})\cong{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{(0)}.

2.8. Approximating C​F+CF^{+}

Following [25], it is useful to have the following approximation to C​F+​(Y)CF^{+}(Y): fix an integer δ≥0\delta\geq 0, let C​Fδ​(Y)⊂C​F+​(Y)CF^{\delta}(Y)\subset CF^{+}(Y) denote the subcomplex which is annihilated by multiplication by Uδ+1U^{\delta+1}, and let H​Fδ​(Y)HF^{\delta}(Y) denote the homology of C​Fδ​(Y)CF^{\delta}(Y). In particular, for δ=0\delta=0, this construction gives H​F^​(Y)\widehat{HF}(Y). Note that for all δ≥0\delta\geq 0, H​Fδ​(Y)HF^{\delta}(Y) is a three-manifold invariant.

3. Construction of the knot filtration

The aim of this section is to construct the knot filtration: a filtration of C​F∞​(Y)CF^{\infty}(Y) induced by a rationally null-homologous knot K⊂YK\subset Y. Most of this discussion is a straightforward generalization of the corresponding constructions for null-homologous knots K⊂YK\subset Y described in [22] and [27].

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a rationally null-homologous knot, and let (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},w,z) be a corresponding doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram.

(10) 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)+(i−j)⋅PD⁡[μ]=ξ.\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x})+(i-j)\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu]=\xi.

∂∞[𝐱,i,j]=∑𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋β∑{ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)|μ⁡(ϕ)=1}#⁡(ℳ⁡(ϕ)ℝ)⋅[𝐲,i−nw​(ϕ),j−nz​(ϕ)],\partial^{\infty}[\mathbf{x},i,j]=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}}\sum_{\{\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\big|\mu(\phi)=1\}}\#\left(\frac{\mathcal{M}(\phi)}{\mathbb{R}}\right)\cdot[\mathbf{y},i-n_{w}(\phi),j-n_{z}(\phi)],

3.1. Relationship with knot Floer homology for null-homologous knots

If K⊂YK\subset Y is a null-homologous knot, then a choice of Seifert surface for YY gives an identification Spinc​(Y,K)≅ℤ⊕Spinc​(Y){\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y,K)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y). Thus, with this additional choice, we identify the Spinc¯​(Y)\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y)-filtration of C​F^​(Y,𝔰)\widehat{CF}(Y,\mathfrak{s}) with a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-filtration. This identification is used, for example, in [22], where the knot filtration is described as a filtration by ℤ\mathbb{Z}, rather than by relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures.

For example, if K¯\overline{K} is a knot in S3S^{3} and ss is an integer, then H^​F​K​(S3,K¯,ξ)\widehat{H}FK(S^{3},\overline{K},\xi) in the present notation corresponds to H^​F​K​(Y,K¯,s)\widehat{H}FK(Y,\overline{K},s) for s∈ℤs\in\mathbb{Z} in the notation from the introduction or  [22], where here ss and ξ\xi are related by c1​(ξ)=2​s​PD​[μ]c_{1}(\xi)=2s\mathrm{PD}[\mu].

The following result is also easy consequences of the proof:

Proposition 4.2.

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a rationally null-homologous knot in a closed, oriented three-manifold, equipped with framing λ\lambda. FWm⋅μ+λ′​(K),𝔰δ:H​Fδ​(Ym⋅μ+λ​(K),𝔱)⟶H​Fδ​(Y)F^{\delta}_{W^{\prime}_{m\cdot\mu+\lambda}(K),\mathfrak{s}}\colon HF^{\delta}(Y_{m\cdot\mu+\lambda}(K),\mathfrak{t})\longrightarrow HF^{\delta}(Y)

is non-trivial. These are the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures 𝔵\mathfrak{x} and 𝔶\mathfrak{y} associated to 𝔱\mathfrak{t} from Theorem 4.1 above.

We return to the proofs of Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.2 after some preliminary discussion and lemmas.

We work with a family of doubly-pointed Heegaard triples for the framed knot K¯\overline{K} (Σ,𝜶,𝜷,𝜸,w,z)(\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$},\mbox{\boldmath$\gamma$},w,z), so that there are identifications Yα,γ≅Ym​μ+λ​(K)Y_{\alpha,\gamma}\cong Y_{m\mu+\lambda}(K), Yβ,γ≅#g−1​(S2×S1)Y_{\beta,\gamma}\cong\#^{g-1}(S^{2}\times S^{1}), Yα,β≅YY_{\alpha,\beta}\cong Y. We can give Heegaard triples for all of the Wm′W^{\prime}_{m} which differ only in γg\gamma_{g}, which winds along the meridian μ\mu. We call this region the “winding region” (c.f. Figure 1 for an illustration of a winding region; in this picture, the subscript for γg\gamma_{g} is dropped).

Definition 4.3.

An intersection point 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋γ\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma} is said to be supported in the winding region if its component along γg\gamma_{g} lies in the winding region. Given 𝐱,𝐲∈𝕋α∩𝕋γ\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\gamma} (both supported in the winding region), we say that ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is supported in the if segment of ∂(𝒟⁡(ϕ))\partial({\mathcal{D}}(\phi)) in γg\gamma_{g} is a subset of the winding region. (Note that if ϕ∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is supported in the winding region, then so is any ϕ′∈π2​(𝐱,𝐲)\phi^{\prime}\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}).) An equivalence class of intersection point for Ym⋅μ+λY_{m\cdot\mu+\lambda} is said to be supported in the winding region if every intersection point in the equivalence class is supported in the winding region, and any two intersection points can be connected by Whitney disks supported in the winding region. Finally, ψ∈π2​(𝐱,Θ,𝐲)\psi\in\pi_{2}(\mathbf{x},\Theta,\mathbf{y}) is said to be a small triangle if the γg\gamma_{g} arc in ∂𝒟⁡(ψ)\partial{\mathcal{D}}(\psi) is supported in the winding region. Note that in this case, 𝐲\mathbf{y} is the “closest point” in 𝕋α∩𝕋β{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta} to 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Definition 4.4.

The depth of a basepoint zz in the winding region is the minimum absolute value of the algebraic intersection number of γg\gamma_{g} with any arc A⊂Σ−α1−…−αgA\subset\Sigma-\alpha_{1}-...-\alpha_{g} which connects zz with some basepoint z0z_{0} outside the winding region with zz. Given an integer ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we say that zz is ϵ\epsilon-centered if its depth is less than or equal to (m−ϵ)/2(m-\epsilon)/2. Similarly, a choice of meridian μ\mu is called ϵ\epsilon-centered if each point z∈μz\in\mu is ϵ\epsilon-centered.

For a Heegaard diagram with an ϵ\epsilon-centered meridian, with basepoints ww and zz on either side of μ\mu. Then, for each small triangle ψ\psi, we have that at least one of nw​(ψ)n_{w}(\psi) or nz​(ψ)=0n_{z}(\psi)=0, and also

5. Künneth principle

Let K¯1⊂Y1\overline{K}_{1}\subset Y_{1} and K¯2⊂Y2\overline{K}_{2}\subset Y_{2} be a pair of oriented three-manifolds equipped with oriented knots. Then, we can form the connected sum to obtain an oriented knot K¯1​#​K¯2⊂Y1​#​Y2\overline{K}_{1}\#\overline{K}_{2}\subset Y_{1}\#Y_{2}. Indeed, given ξi∈Spinc¯​(Yi,Ki)\xi_{i}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{i},K_{i}), we can form their connected sum ξ1​#​ξ2\xi_{1}\#\xi_{2}. This induces a gluing map

Spinc¯​(Y1,K1)×Spinc¯​(Y2,K2)⟶Spinc¯​(Y1​#​Y2,K1​#​K2),\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{1},K_{1})\times\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{2},K_{2})\longrightarrow\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{1}\#Y_{2},K_{1}\#K_{2}),

written ξ1,ξ2↦ξ1​#​ξ2\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\mapsto\xi_{1}\#\xi_{2}. which is equivariant with respect to the natural map

H2​(Y1,K1,ℤ)⊕H2​(Y2,K2,ℤ)⟶H2​(Y1​#​Y2,K1​#​K2,ℤ).H^{2}(Y_{1},K_{1};\mathbb{Z})\oplus H^{2}(Y_{2},K_{2};\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow H^{2}(Y_{1}\#Y_{2},K_{1}\#K_{2};\mathbb{Z}).

More explicitly, we can think of ξi\xi_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) as specified by a non-vanishing vector field which contains K¯i\overline{K}_{i} as a closed orbit. We realize the connected sum as attaching a one-handle to Y1​∐Y2Y_{1}\coprod Y_{2} along a pair of three-balls BiB_{i} supported on K¯i\overline{K}_{i}. We can assume that on each sphere Si=∂BiS_{i}=\partial B_{i}, there are eactly two points where the vector field is normal to SiS_{i}, the two points where SiS_{i} meets K¯i\overline{K}_{i}: the “in-going” and “out-going points”. Here, p∈Sip\in S_{i} is “in-going” if ξi\xi_{i} points into Yi−BiY_{i}-B_{i}. We can then match the in-going point on Y1−B1Y_{1}-B_{1} with the out-going point on Y2−B2Y_{2}-B_{2} and vice versa, to construct a nowhere vanishing vector field on Y1​#​Y2Y_{1}\#Y_{2}. This new vector field has K1​#​K2K_{1}\#K_{2} as a closed orbit, and it has prescribed from in the connected sum region. This vector field gives rise to a relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure Spinc​(Y1​#​Y2,K¯1​#​K¯2){\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y_{1}\#Y_{2},\overline{K}_{1}\#\overline{K}_{2}), inducing the gluing map above.

The gluing map can be described in terms of Heegaard diagrams as follows. Let (Σ1,𝜶1,𝜷1,w1,z1)(\Sigma_{1},\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}_{1},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{1},w_{1},z_{1}) and (Σ2,𝜶2,𝜷2,w2,z2)(\Sigma_{2},\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}_{2},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{2},w_{2},z_{2}) be the doubly-pointed Heegaard diagrams compatible with the oriented knots K¯1⊂Y1\overline{K}_{1}\subset Y_{1} and K¯2⊂Y2\overline{K}_{2}\subset Y_{2}. Consider the oriented two-manifold Σ3\Sigma_{3} obtained as the connected sum of Σ1\Sigma_{1} with Σ2\Sigma_{2}, identifying neighborhoods of z1z_{1} with w2w_{2}. Then, the doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram (Σ3,𝜶1∪𝜶2,𝜷1∪𝜷2,w1,z2)(\Sigma_{3},\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}_{1}\cup\mbox{\boldmath$\alpha$}_{2},\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{1}\cup\mbox{\boldmath$\beta$}_{2},w_{1},z_{2}) is compatible with K¯1​#​K¯2⊂Y1​#​Y2\overline{K}_{1}\#\overline{K}_{2}\subset Y_{1}\#Y_{2}. Now, given 𝐱1∈𝕋α1∩𝕋β1\mathbf{x}_{1}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha_{1}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta_{1}} and 𝐱2∈𝕋α2∩𝕋β2\mathbf{x}_{2}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha_{2}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta_{2}}, we can think of 𝐱1×𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{1}\times\mathbf{x}_{2} as an intersection point 𝕋α1∪α2∩𝕋β1∪β2{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha_{1}\cup\alpha_{2}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta_{1}\cup\beta_{2}}. Then,

𝔰¯w1,z2​(𝐱1×𝐱2)=𝔰¯w1,z1​(𝐱1)​#​𝔰¯w2,z2​(𝐱2).\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w_{1},z_{2}}(\mathbf{x}_{1}\times\mathbf{x}_{2})=\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w_{1},z_{1}}(\mathbf{x}_{1})\#\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w_{2},z_{2}}(\mathbf{x}_{2}).

The following is a straightforward generalization of the connected sum principle for knot homology in the case of null-homologous knots, c.f. [22], [27]. A proof can be found, for example, in Theorem  of [22]; we omit it here.

Theorem 5.1.

Fix ξi∈Spinc¯​(Yi,Ki)\xi_{i}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{i},K_{i}) for i=1,2i=1,2. There is a filtered chain homotopy equivalence

C​F​K∞​(Y1,K1,ξ1)⊗ℤ⁡[U]C​F​K∞​(Y2,K2,ξ2)⟶C​F​K∞​(Y1​#​Y2,K1​#​K2,ξ1​#​ξ2).CFK^{\infty}(Y_{1},K_{1},\xi_{1})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[U]}CFK^{\infty}(Y_{2},K_{2},\xi_{2})\ \longrightarrow CFK^{\infty}(Y_{1}\#Y_{2},K_{1}\#K_{2},\xi_{1}\#\xi_{2}).
Definition 5.2.

A UU-knot is a knot in a three-manifold YY with the property that the induced filtration of C​F∞​(Y,𝔰)CF^{\infty}(Y,\mathfrak{s}) is trivial. More precisely, given any ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K)\xi\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,K), C​F​K∞​(Y,K,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y,K,\xi) is chain homotopy equivalent via a relatively ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered chain homotopy to the chain complex RR which is a free, rank one ℤ⁡[U,U−1]\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}] module with the trivial differential.

The unknot in S3S^{3} is a UU-knot. Indeed, the results of [21] can be interpreted as saying that the only UU-knot in S3S^{3} is the unknot. Other UU-knots will be described in Lemma 7.1.

Corollary 5.3.

If K2⊂Y2K_{2}\subset Y_{2} is a UU-knot, then for each ξ1∈Spinc¯​(Y1,K¯1)\xi_{1}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{1},\overline{K}_{1}) and 𝔰2∈Spinc​(Y2)\mathfrak{s}_{2}\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y_{2}), there is some ξ2∈Spinc¯​(Y2)\xi_{2}\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{2}) representing 𝔰2\mathfrak{s}_{2}, with the property that

C​F​K∞​(Y1,K¯1,ξ1)≅C​F​K∞​(Y1​#​Y2,K¯1​#​K¯2,ξ1​#​ξ2)CFK^{\infty}(Y_{1},\overline{K}_{1},\xi_{1})\cong CFK^{\infty}(Y_{1}\#Y_{2},\overline{K}_{1}\#\overline{K}_{2},\xi_{1}\#\xi_{2})

as ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered chain complexes.

Proof. Let ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y2)\xi\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{2}) be any relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure representing 𝔰2\mathfrak{s}_{2}. Then, C​F​K∞​(Y2,K¯2,ξ)CFK^{\infty}(Y_{2},\overline{K}_{2},\xi) is quasi-isomorphic to the ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}-filtered chain complex ℤ⁡[U,U−1]\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}] which contains a non-trivial element in filtration (0,n)(0,n) for some nn. Letting

ξ2=ξ+n​PD​[μ]\xi_{2}=\xi+n\mathrm{PD}[\mu]

(where μ\mu of course is a meridian for K2K_{2}), we see that C​F​K∞​(Y2,K¯2,ξ2)CFK^{\infty}(Y_{2},\overline{K}_{2},\xi_{2}) is quasi-isomorphic to ℤ⁡[U,U−1]\mathbb{Z}[U,U^{-1}] with a generator in filtration level (0,0)(0,0) (c.f. Proposition 3.2). For this choice of ξ2\xi_{2}, the corollary is an immediate consequence of Theorem 5.1.           

6. The Morse surgery formula

We describe the Morse surgery formula, which expresses the Heegaard Floer homologies of Morse surgery along a rationally null-homologous knot in terms of its knot Floer homology.

Given 𝔰∈Spinc​(Yλ​(K))\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y_{\lambda}(K)), let

𝔸𝔰+​(Y,K¯)\displaystyle{\mathbb{A}}^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}(Y,\overline{K}) =\displaystyle= ⨁{ξ∈Spinc¯​(Yλ​(K),K¯)|GYλ​(K),K¯​(ξ)=𝔰}Aξ+​(Y,K¯)\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\{\xi\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K})\big|G_{Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K}}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}\}}{A}^{+}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K})
𝔹𝔰+​(Y,K¯)\displaystyle{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}(Y,\overline{K}) =\displaystyle= ⨁{ξ∈Spinc¯​(Yλ​(K),K¯)|GYλ​(K),K¯​(ξ)=𝔰}Bξ+​(Y,K¯),\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\{\xi\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K})\big|G_{Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K}}(\xi)=\mathfrak{s}\}}{B}^{+}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K}),

where here Aξ+​(Y,K¯){A}^{+}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K}) and Bξ+​(Y,K¯){B}^{+}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K}) are defined as in Equation (12).

In the above definition, we view KK also as a knot in Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K). An orientation on K⊂YK\subset Y naturally induces also an orientation on the induced knot in Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K) in a natural way: an orientation on KK corresponds to an orientation on a meridian for KK, which can be thought of as supported in Y−nd⁡(K)Y-{\mathrm{nd}}(K), which in turn can be thought of as a subset of Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K), where it in turn induces an orientation of the induced knot in Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K).

Theorem 6.1.

Let K⊂YK\subset Y be a knot in a rational homology three-sphere, and let λ\lambda be a framing on KK with the property that Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K) is also a rational homology three-sphere. The Heegaard Floer homology H​F+​(Yλ​(K),𝔰)HF^{+}(Y_{\lambda}(K),\mathfrak{s}) is calculated by the homology of the mapping cone of the chain map

D𝔰+:𝔸𝔰+​(Y,K¯)⟶𝔹𝔰+​(Y,K¯)D^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}(Y,\overline{K})\longrightarrow{\mathbb{B}}^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}(Y,\overline{K})

D𝔰+​({aξ}ξ∈GYλ​(K),K¯−1​(𝔰))={bξ}ξ∈GYλ​(K),K¯−1​(𝔰),D^{+}_{\mathfrak{s}}\left(\{a_{\xi}\}_{\xi\in G_{Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K}}^{-1}(\mathfrak{s})}\right)=\{b_{\xi}\}_{\xi\in G_{Y_{\lambda}(K),\overline{K}}^{-1}(\mathfrak{s})},

bξ=hξ−PD⁡[Kλ]+​(aξ−PD⁡[Kλ])−vξ+​(aξ).b_{\xi}=h^{+}_{\xi-\mathrm{PD}[K_{\lambda}]}(a_{\xi-\mathrm{PD}[K_{\lambda}]})-v^{+}_{\xi}(a_{\xi}).

The proof is modeled on the proof of the main result from [25]. Specifically, it is based on two key ingredients: the relationship between the knot Floer homology of K⊂YK\subset Y and the Heegaard Floer homology of three-manifolds obtained as sufficiently large surgeries on KK from Section 4, and also an exact exact triangle which relates, for all integers mm, the Heegaard Floer homologies of Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K), Ym⋅μ+λ​(K)Y_{m\cdot\mu+\lambda}(K), and YY (the latter taken with twisted coefficients).

We have not strived for maximal generality in Theorem 6.1. As a technical tool, we make heavy use of the rational grading on H​F+HF^{+} which is defined on the Heegaard Floer homology of any three-manifold equipped with a Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure whose first Chern class is torsion, cf. Section  of [14]. Thus, Theorem 6.1 holds – and indeed the proof we give below applies – whenever we consider Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures over Yλ​(K)Y_{\lambda}(K) whose first Chern class is torsion.

Theorem 6.4.

The group C​Fδ​(Yλ​(K),𝔰)CF^{\delta}(Y_{\lambda}(K),\mathfrak{s}) is quasi-ismorphic to the mapping cone 𝕏𝔰δ​(λ){\mathbb{X}}^{\delta}_{\mathfrak{s}}(\lambda) of

We deduce Theorem 6.4 from a combination of Theorems 6.2 and 4.1. Theorem 6.1 will follow from Theorem 6.4, together with some further observations about gradings, as explained in Subsection 6.3.

We turn our attention now towards proving Theorem 6.4. We assume that both dd and nn have the same sign, and hence without additional loss of generality that both are positive, returning to the case where their signs are opposite in Subsection 6.4.

It will be useful to have the following lemma. In the statement, “sufficiently large” is meant with respect to the ordering on Spinc​(Y,K){\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y,K) with fixed filling 𝔱\mathfrak{t} over YY described earlier. Specifically, recall that ξ1≤ξ2\xi_{1}\leq\xi_{2} if ξ2=ξ1+j⋅PD⁡[μ]\xi_{2}=\xi_{1}+j\cdot\mathrm{PD}[\mu] for some j≥0j\geq 0. In particular, we say that a condition PP holds for all all sufficiently large relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structures Spinc¯​(Y,K¯)\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,\overline{K}) if there is a finite collection Ξ⊂Spinc¯​(Y,K¯)\Xi\subset\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,\overline{K}) with the properties that each 𝔱∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{t}\in{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(Y) can be represented by some η∈Spinc¯​(Y,K¯)\eta\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,\overline{K}) with η∈Ξ\eta\in\Xi, and also for any ξ∈Spinc¯​(Y,K¯)\xi\in\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y,\overline{K}) which has the property that ξ≥η\xi\geq\eta for some η∈Ξ\eta\in\Xi then PP holds for ξ\xi.

Lemma 6.5.

If ξ\xi is sufficiently large, then

vξδ:Aξδ​(Y,K¯)⟶Bξδ​(Y,K¯)v^{\delta}_{\xi}\colon{A}^{\delta}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K})\longrightarrow{B}^{\delta}_{\xi}(Y,\overline{K})

is trivial; moreover, if ξ\xi is sufficiently small, then hξδh^{\delta}_{\xi} is an isomorphism, while vξδv^{\delta}_{\xi} is trivial.

Proof. Since there are finitely many 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}, there is a maximal ξ0\xi_{0} among all 𝔰¯w,z​(𝐱)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(\mathbf{x}) with 𝐱∈𝕋α∩𝕋β\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha}\cap{\mathbb{T}}_{\beta}. 7. The proof of Theorem 1.1

If K⊂YK\subset Y is a null-homologous knot, then Yp/q​(K)Y_{p/q}(K) can be realized by surgery with coefficient aa inside the knot K​#​Oq/r⊂Y​#​L​(q,r)K\#O_{q/r}\subset Y\#L(q,r), where aa is the greatest integer smaller than or equal to p/qp/q, a=⌊pq⌋a=\lfloor\frac{p}{q}\rfloor, and

pq=a+rq,\frac{p}{q}=a+\frac{r}{q},

and Oq/r⊂L⁡(q,r)O_{q/r}\subset L(q,r) is the knot which is obtained by viewing one component of the Hopf link as a knot inside the lens space L⁡(q,r)L(q,r), thought of as q/rq/r surgery on the other component of the Hopf link, c.f. Figure 2.

In view of these remarks, Theorem 1.1 is proved by combining a model calculation of the knot Floer homology of Oq/rO_{q/r}, the Künneth principle for connected sums, together with the surgery formula of Theorem 6.1.

Of course, L⁡(q,r)−Oq/rL(q,r)-O_{q/r} is a solid torus, and consequently, there is an affine identification Spinc¯​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r)≅ℤ\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(L(q,r),O_{q/r})\cong\mathbb{Z}.

Lemma 7.1.

The knot Oq/r⊂L⁡(q,r)O_{q/r}\subset L(q,r) is a UU-knot. Indeed, there is an affine identification ϕ\phi fitting into a commutative diagram

ℤ→ϕSpinc¯​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r)↓↓GL⁡(q,r),Oq/rℤ/q​ℤ→≅Spinc​(L​(q,r))\begin{CD}\mathbb{Z}@>{\phi}>{}>\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(L(q,r),O_{q/r})\\ @V{}V{}V@V{}V{G_{L(q,r),O_{q/r}}}V\\ \mathbb{Z}/{q}\mathbb{Z}@>{\cong}>{}>{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}(L(q,r))\end{CD}

(where the left vertical arrow is the natural quotient map) with the property that

H^​F​K​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r,ϕ⁡(i))≅{ℤif 0≤i≤q−10otherwise.\widehat{H}FK(L(q,r),O_{q/r},\phi(i))\cong\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathbb{Z}&{\text{if $0\leq i\leq q-1$}}\\ 0&{\text{otherwise.}}\end{array}\right.

Proof. Consider the standard genus one Heegaard decomposition of the lens space L⁡(q,r)L(q,r), where α\alpha is a curve of slope 0/10/1 and β\beta is a curve of slope q/rq/r. Placing two basepoints ww and zz, separated by an arc which is disjoint from α\alpha and meets β\beta exactly once, we obtain a doubly-pointed Heegaard diagram for Oq/r⊂L⁡(q,r)O_{q/r}\subset L(q,r). Of course α∩β\alpha\cap\beta consists of exactly qq points {x0,…,xq−1}\{x_{0},...,x_{q-1}\}, each one representing a different Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c} structure over L⁡(q,r)L(q,r). See Figure 3 for an illustration.

Now,

(28) H1​(L⁡(q,r)−Oq/r)≅H1​(T2−w−z)ℤ⋅α+ℤ⋅β≅H1​(T2)ℤ⋅α≅ℤ,H_{1}(L(q,r)-O_{q/r})\cong\frac{H_{1}(T^{2}-w-z)}{\mathbb{Z}\cdot\alpha+\mathbb{Z}\cdot\beta}\cong\frac{H_{1}(T^{2})}{\mathbb{Z}\cdot\alpha}\cong\mathbb{Z},

which is generated by the homology class represented by a curve γ\gamma in T2T^{2} with slope 1/01/0. We specify an ordering on the {xi}i=0q−1\{x_{i}\}_{i=0}^{q-1} as follows. Let mm be the intersection point of β\beta with the arc connecting ww and zz. Our ordering is specified by the conditions that the arc in β\beta from xix_{i} to xi+1x_{i+1} is disjoint from all the other xkx_{k} and mm. Clearly, with this ordering, ϵ⁡(xi,xi+1)=γ\epsilon(x_{i},x_{i+1})=\gamma. Let ϕ⁡(i)\phi(i) correspond to 𝔰¯w,z​(xi)\underline{\mathfrak{s}}_{w,z}(x_{i}). The lemma follows.           

Suppose that KK is a null-homologous knot in an integral homology three-sphere YY. In this case, H2​(Y,K)≅ℤH^{2}(Y,K)\cong\mathbb{Z}, and also H2​(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r)≅ℤH^{2}(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r})\cong\mathbb{Z}.

Lemma 7.2.

Suppose that K⊂YK\subset Y is a null-homologous knot in an integer homology three-sphere. Under the connected sum

(Y,K)​#​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r)⟶(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r),(Y,K)\#(L(q,r),O_{q/r})\longrightarrow(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r}),

the following diagram commutes:

ℤ⊕ℤ→fℤ≅↓↓≅H2​(Y,K)⊕H2​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r)→H2​(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r),\begin{CD}\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}@>{f}>{}>\mathbb{Z}\\ @V{\cong}V{}V@V{}V{\cong}V\\ H^{2}(Y,K)\oplus H^{2}(L(q,r),O_{q/r})@>{}>{}>H^{2}(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r}),\\ \end{CD}

where f⁡(x,y)=q​x+yf(x,y)=qx+y. Proof. Let mm and ℓ\ell denote the meridian and the longitude of Oq/rO_{q/r}. We have an isomorphism H2​(L⁡(q,r),Oq/r)≅ℤH^{2}(L(q,r),O_{q/r})\cong\mathbb{Z} under which mm and ℓ\ell are mapped to rr and qq respectively. Now in Y​#​L​(q,r)−K​#​Oq/rY\#L(q,r)-K\#O_{q/r}, clearly the meridian of KK is homologous to a longitude for Oq/rO_{q/r}, and hence it is mapped to qq under the isomorphism.

Moreover, the push-off of KλK_{\lambda} is homologous m+a​ℓm+a\ell, which in turn is mapped to r+a​q=pr+aq=p, under this above map.           

Proof of Theorem 1.1. Fix an identification Spinc¯​(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r)≅ℤ\underline{{\mathrm{Spin}}^{c}}(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r})\cong\mathbb{Z}, and correspondingly think of As+​(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r){A}^{+}_{s}(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r}) as indexed by s∈ℤs\in\mathbb{Z}. for some g:ℤ⟶ℤg\colon\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z} (where here ≃\simeq means filtered quasi-isomorphic). Indeed, according to Lemma 7.2, the formula g⁡(s)g(s) satisfies s=q​g​(s)+js=qg(s)+j where, according to Lemma 7.1, 0≤j<q0\leq j<q; i.e.

g⁡(s)=⌊sq⌋.g(s)=\lfloor\frac{s}{q}\rfloor.

Recall also that PD⁡[Kλ]\mathrm{PD}[K_{\lambda}] represents pp times a generator of H2​(Y​#​L​(q,r),K​#​Oq/r)H^{2}(Y\#L(q,r),K\#O_{q/r}).

With these remarks in place, Theorem 1.1 is obtained as a direct application of Theorem 6.1. ∎

7.1. The case of H​F^\widehat{HF}

Some of the algebra is simpler when one considers H​F+HF^{+}, rather than H​F^\widehat{HF}. To this end, we let

i.e.

D^i,p/q​{a⌊i+p​sq⌋}s∈ℤ={b⌊i+p​sq⌋}s∈ℤ,{\widehat{D}}_{i,p/q}\{a_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}=\{b_{\lfloor\frac{i+ps}{q}\rfloor}\}_{s\in\mathbb{Z}},
